name: Alexander
description:
The Alexander cocktail was born in London in 1922 in honor of a famous bride, at the beginning it was called Panama, Gin was used instead of Cognac and light cocoa cream instead of dark.

Throughout its history, Alexander has given rise to many other variations:

**Grasshopper**: This variant is also part of the Iba list and involves the use of crème de menthe verde instead of cognac.

**Alexandra**: Use the light cocoa cream instead of the dark one and replace the nutmeg with cocoa.

**Alexander’s Sister**: Use crème de menthe instead of crème de cacao

**Alejandro**: Replace cognac with rum

Its distinctive flavor can be incorporated into numerous cocktails, but it’s best known for the Amaretto Sour, a drink that tends to get a bad rap. That’s because, too often, the cocktail is overly sweet and relies on premade sour mix.
instructions:

name: Amaretto Sour with Cask-Proof Whiskey
description:
There are two things that impede all other Amaretto Sours from challenging mine. First off, the obvious: they’re too sweet. One does not simply use an everyday sour recipe to make a world-class Amaretto Sour, it must be adjusted for this particular liqueur.

Second, and this is a big one: amaretto isn’t strong enough on its own to stand up to a bunch of other ingredients. It’s weak. It needs help. And for this, I enlist the assistance of an old friend. One that knows amaretto’s strengths and weaknesses. Or, mainly, its weaknesses. One that works with amaretto, to complete it like Jerry Maguire completes Rene Zellwiger’s character, whatever her name was. And that, my friends, is cask-proof bourbon.

name: Americano
description:
The story of the Americano dates back to the second half of the 1800s in Milan.  Over the years the cocktail acquires notoriety thanks to some homages from the world of cinema, including James Bond (007 Casino Royale) whose favorite cocktail was, precisely, the Americano.

The nickname “American” was born when Primo Carnera, a giant Italian boxer, became world heavyweight champion at Madison Square Garden in New York.  When Carnera returned to Italy with the title, he was greeted with this very Italian cocktail which, for the occasion, was called “Americano”.

The Americano entered the IBA Cocktail List only in 1987 but, in reality, it was a cocktail that spread all over Italy during the 1930s.

name: Andalusian Buck
description: This drink is great because it doesn’t go too far any any direction. It’s not too sweet, there’s only a teaspoon of sugar in the whole thing. It’s not too sour, there’a barely half a lime’s worth of juice. And it’s not too strong, it only calls for an ounce of gin. And between the ginger beer and the Amontillado sherry, it’s absolutely bursting with flavor. In sort, it’s refreshing and crushable, but still interesting.

2. Shake until cold.
3. I like to add the ginger beer directly to the shaker, then pour slowly over fresh ice in a chilled Collins glass.

name: Angel Face
description:
Although the origin of the cocktail is not known, the main hypotheses assume that it was born in the twenties of the twentieth century in France: this thesis would prove the presence of calvados, a liqueur commonly used in France and, in particular, in that period, as an epidemic of phylloxera in European vineyards had limited the production of brandy.
On this basis, one of the most frequent hypotheses has it that the cocktail was created in Paris on July 19, 1919, in honor of the celebrations for the victory of the First World War.
The first reliable evidence, however, dates back to 1930. Some sources indicate that the name derives from that of an American gangster active during Prohibition; less likely the dedication to Rick Blaine, the protagonist of Casablanca played by Humphrey Bogart, as the film follows the first testimonies (1942).

The recipe is simple: there's no fussy bar prep or homemade ingredients involved. But to keep the flavors balanced, use an agave-forward mezcal versus an "overly smokey one" so as not to overpower the amari's herbaceousness.

The Spritz became widely popular outside of Italy around 2018 and Aperol Spritz was ranked as the world's ninth bestselling cocktail in 2019 by the website Drinks International.

name: Appetizer à l’Italienne
description:
It could be argued that the difference between a forgotten cocktail and a beloved classic is simply the size of the audience. The Appetizer à l’Italienne appeared in 1892, then largely disappeared. (A similar recipe, for the absinthe-free Bonsoni Cocktail, appeared in 1917.) With its aggressive match of sweet vermouth and Fernet-Branca accented with absinthe, the cocktail’s character is rooted in the late 19th century, and out of place in the 20th.

But the cocktail renaissance brought both a taste for bold, bitter combinations, and an interest in historical spelunking.

To balance the brawn of fernet and absinthe, it’s important to use a richer style of vermouth, such as Carpano Antica Formula or a Vermouth di Torino. And don’t skip the simple syrup: the sugar converts fernet from a digestif to an aperitif, as suggested by the drink’s name.

 ## Editors note:

### White Chocolate Eggshell

Temper high-quality white chocolate. While the chocolate is heating, blow up water balloons to roughly the size of an extra-large egg, and assemble a cold water bath. 

When the white chocolate is tempered, dip the balloon halfway and allow the chocolate to drip off, then place directly into the cold water to set.

Once the chocolate has set, pop the balloon with a paring knife or scissors, and peel it away from the chocolate shell. Chocolate eggs may be stored in the freezer until ready to use.

The spirit base is pisco, which offers distinct grape notes, subtle floral and fruity flavors that pair well with the sweet, nutty amaretto. Passion fruit pulp gives the drink a tiki-like direction with a balanced sweet-tart fruitiness, while agave nectar and lemon juice add a floral tartness. Egg whites provide a foamy, decadent texture. It is a deliciously complex and fruity cocktail, suitable for garden parties and summer gatherings.

name: Aviation
description:
Aviation was created in New York around 1916, shortly before the start of American Prohibition.

Lately the aviation recipe was found in a 1911 magazine, so the recipe is thought to have been born earlier then 1916.

The original recipe indicates the type of Gin to be used ‘El Bart Gin “and the recipe is made up in addition to gin, with lemon juice, maraschino and Creme di Violette.

The recipe is found again in 1930 but without the Creme de Violette, this probably due to the difficulty of finding the violet cream during the post-war period In the 1960s it was still unavailable and therefore, simply, the basic ingredient of the Aviation cocktail was discontinued and the bartenders definitively gave up the characteristic blue color of the drink.

The IBA proposes it today in its original version with the creme de violette which is now on the market again.  This fragrant ingredient not only gave the mix a sweetly floral taste, but also gave it a beautiful sky blue color.
instructions:

On April 28, 1936 the New York Supreme Court ruled that the drink must contain Bacardí rum in order to be called a Bacardí cocktail.

name: Banana Daiquiri
description: Popular at tropical bars and often sold in prefabricated mixes, blended versions of the classic Daiquiri rarely garner the same respect as their three-ingredient forebears. It’s a shame because a properly made Banana Daiquiri is bright and balanced. This Banana Daiquiri recipe is made with aged rum, tart lime, and a carefully calibrated combination of banana liqueur and fresh bananas. Those fresh bananas are treated with care. Ideally the chunked fruit is kept at 17 degrees Fahrenheit, whereas most household freezers are set to 0 degrees Fahrenheit, so they blend evenly and require less ice to reach frothy perfection. To mimic this at home, let fully frozen pieces of fruit sit at room temperature for approximately 10 minutes on the kitchen counter, then pop everything into a blender and set sail.

You can experiment with whatever Fernet you have on hand, but Fernet-Vallet will bring a deeper bark-like dryness to the mix.

name: Bee’s Knees
description:
The Bee's Knees dates to Paris in 1921.

The name comes from prohibition-era slang meaning "the best".
instructions:
1. Stir honey with lemon and orange juices until it dissolves
2. Add gin and shake with ice
3. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass

**Variations:**
- Barr Hill Gin is sometimes recommended for its honey infusion, though other gins may be used (including Barr Hill's Tom Cat gin).
- The honey may be diluted 1:1 with warm water to thin the consistency.
- The honey may be diluted 1:1 with simple syrup instead of water.
- A sprig of basil or thyme may be used for garnish instead of lemon peel.

name: Beet It
description: This mezcal beet cocktail drinks like an earthy, vegetal Margarita. Garnishing the cocktail with drops of olive oil enhances its savory character while also giving it a velvety mouthfeel.
instructions:

3. Serve up, into a coupe or martini glass.
4. Top with drops of olive oil.

**Note:** No prebottled beet juice will live up to freshly juiced beets. If you don't have your own juicer at home, the best option is to swing by your local fresh juice shop and have them make you a fresh batch. A 16-oz. to-go cup will make 16 cocktails. Natural grocery stores carry decent bottled beet juice, but they generally add acid in the form of lemon juice and citric acid as a preservative, in which case you can pull back on the amount of lime juice to keep the cocktail balanced.

name: Belleville

name: Beton
description: The Beton is a Czech cocktail starring Becherovka, an herbal liqueur, and tonic water, that is sometimes compared to a Gin and Tonic.
instructions:

name: Betty Carter
description:
Most whiskey and bourbon-based cocktails are synonymous with the cold time of the year, when one turns to the warming qualities of these spirits. Betty Carter, on the other hand, hits a nice middle ground, possessing enough refreshing qualities making it very suitable for the warm periods as well.

Base of the cocktail is bourbon with strong notes of oak, vanilla and caramel. It is then paired with sweet profile of PX sherry and its signature intense fruity notes like figs and dates, giving the cocktail a little lightness. This bright impression is then further reinforced by a healthy does of tart lemon juice, changing the overall flavour profile closer to a sour cocktail style. Touch of amaro Nonino, gives the cocktail a further complexity with delicate sweet orange notes balanced by the bitterness of gentian root and quinine.

Betty Carter, is a cocktail with a pretty straight forward build, just requiring to source a somewhat harder to get amaro, but once you have it you are good to go. Simple to make, delicious and remarkably refreshing. Suitable to drink all year round, although for the winter period, I would probably add a little bit of simple syrup to reign in the tartness, or look for a slightly sweeter and bolder PX Sherry.
instructions:
1. Combine all of the ingredients in a cocktail shaker.
2. Add ice and shake until chilled.
3. Double strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
garnish: Garnish with an orange twist and a sprig of mint.

name: Betty Is Back
description: Named for a head bartender of the 1940s, this sparkler dates to 2008. Betty is Back is a dry, bubbly sip with delicate floral and citrus notes from a complex blend of Aperol and elderflower liqueurs and fresh lemon juice, while the Champagne raises a toast to this memorable wartime bartender.
instructions: 1. Combine all of the ingredients, except the Champagne, in a mixing glass filled with ice and stir until well chilled. Strain into a flute and gently pour in the Champagne. Garnish.

name: Between the Sheets
description: The origin of the cocktail is usually placed in Paris in the 1930s as a derivative of the sidecar. However, competing theories exist that claim the cocktail was created in approximately 1921, or in French brothels as an apéritif for consumption by the prostitutes.
instructions:
1. Add all ingredients into a cocktail shaker
2. Shake with ice and strain into a chilled cocktail glass

name: Beuser & Angus Special
description: Chartreuse sour from Berlin, the Beuser & Angus Special takes inspiration from the Last Word and the Ramos Gin Fizz. Created in 2007, the drink has gone on to become a modern classic.

instructions: Stir in mixing glass with ice and strain

description: A modern take on the Bijou, this cocktail recipe puts a fresh spin on the classic Chartreuse cocktail, similar to a White Negroni.
instructions:

3. Strain into a rocks glass over ice.
4. Garnish with a lemon peel “flag.”

name: Bitter Giuseppe
description: First served in Chicago, the Bitter Giuseppe cocktail has become a modern classic over the years, with iterations popping up on menus at places like Cure in New Orleans, Elske and Ludlow Liquors in Chicago.
instructions:

name: Cable Car
description:
The Cable Car cocktail pays tribute to San Francisco's cable cars! The cable cars of San Francisco are an icon of a past era. They still climb the hills of San Francisco and carry commuters and tourists up and down busy streets.

This rum sour is sweet, tart, and lightly spiced, regardless of whether you are familiar with its name. The Cable Car cocktail is a modified Sidecar. It substitutes brandy with spiced rum, back then, spiced rum was very uncommon.

Captain Morgan was probably the most widely available spiced rum label at the time of Cable Car's inception. The Captain is probably still the most well-known of the category, but today there are plenty of other options. A more luxurious approach is to maybe use something like a Boukman Botanical Rhum.

Similar to a Sidecar or Brandy Crusta, the Cable Car includes an orange liqueur in addition to simple syrup for sweetness--specifically, orange curacao. using Bol's or something similar can make the drink heavy, so it's better to use a dry curacao. The original recipe uses Marie Brizard Orange Curacao. Grand Marnier or maybe Cointreau would also work great.

Another aspect that made the Cable Car a classic is the way it was presented. A mixture of cinnamon and sugar gives the drink a punchier sweetness and a present hint of spice.

name: Carajillo
description: Bolstering one’s coffee with a shot of booze is more or less a universally accepted practice, regardless of time of day or occasion. The exact origins of Spain’s version, the Carajillo, remain up for debate. Some point to Spanish soldiers in Cuba adding rum to their coffee to muster the coraje needed for battle, while others have suggested the drink’s roots are in southern Spain’s Andalusia region, with the name derived from the Spanish expletive carajo. It’s perhaps a fitting sentiment while doctoring your cup—why not? The drink has since migrated overseas, becoming popular in Latin American countries and Mexico City in particular, where a Carajillo recipe can be found on virtually any bar menu. The go-to booze these days is also a Spanish export, Licor 43—a sweet, botanical liqueur with notes of vanilla and citrus—thanks to savvy marketing by the brand. The stateside popularity of Espresso Martinis and their ilk have extended an affinity for coffee-based cocktails more broadly, making the Carajillo cocktail a perfect two-ingredient fit for any hour of the day.
instructions:
1. Brew 3 oz. of espresso per drink and cool to room temperature or chill in
the fridge to prevent excess dilution. In a shaker filled with ice, add chilled espresso and Licor 43. Shake well until creamy and frothy, then strain into the glass filled with fresh ice, and garnish.
TIPThe Carajillo is as much a coffee drink as it is a cocktail—brewing the espresso fresh, and using a high-quality coffee, will have a big impact on the final flavor.

name: Caribbean Ember
description:
Tiki cocktails and whiskey is far from traditional cocktail combination. However, Caribbean Ember brings it together masterfully and with a great and delicious effect.

Cocktail is built around the blend of dark rum and rye whiskey. Dark rum contributes rich molasses, caramel, dried fruit notes, while whiskey adds some oaky, peppery spiciness, resulting in a one-of-a-kind cocktail base. Splash of pineapple juice, pays homage to the tiki culture with distinct sweet-tart fruitiness, while a touch of lime juice and maple syrup, expands the flavours of rum and whiskey. All of these notes are then wrapped up by the warming spiciness of ginger beer, providing not only freshness, but also balancing the cocktail out. A few dashes of Angostura bitters bring it all together and imparts more tropical notes bridging the gap between old-fashioned and tiki styles.

Caribbean Ember is a unique and intriguing cocktail. Many have tried to incorporate whiskey into a tropical drink, but most of these attempts have failed, Caribbean Ember is the rare exception.

garnish: Garnish with orange zest and maraschino cherry.

name: Charles Dickens’ Punch
description: Dickens was a dedicated punch-maker and an inveterate showman, as this historic flaming punch proves. And with a simple list of ingredients and some fireproof tools, you, too, can add some razzle dazzle to your own holiday gathering. Be sure to use a heatproof bowl with a capacity of at least one gallon.
instructions:
1. A few hours before preparing the punch, peel 4 lemons with a vegetable peeler or paring knife to create 4 long spirals of peel. Put them in a heatproof bowl with 3/4 of a cup of demerara sugar. Muddle the peels and
the sugar together and let sit at room temperature. Juice the 4 peeled lemons (and any extra needed) through a strainer to yield 6 oz. of strained juice. Set aside in the fridge.
2. Measure the rum and Cognac into a pitcher or other pouring vessel. To prepare the punch, boil the water and place the bowl containing the lemon peels and sugar on a wooden cutting board or other heat-resistant surface in an open area (free from clutter, flammable items, or nearby curtains or light fixtures) where everyone can gather around at a safe distance.
3. Pour the Cognac and rum into the bowl. Use a long-handled barspoon to remove a spoonful of the rum-cognac mixture. Light the spoonful on fire with a match and hold it just above the surface of the bowl in order to ignite the rest of the liquid. Stir with the barspoon or a heatproof ladle to help dissolve the sugar. Let the mixture burn for 2 or 3 minutes, occasionally lifting out one of the lemon peels with the ladle or spoon to show the flames running down it.
4. Cover the bowl with a large heatproof dish or tray to extinguish the flames. Add the lemon juice and the hot water. (For cold punch, replace the hot water with 3 cups of cold water and add a 1-quart block of ice, made by freezing a quart bowl of water for 24 hours.) Stir. Grate fresh nutmeg over the top and ladle out in 3-ounce servings.

name: Chauncey
description: Equal-parts gin, Cognac and rye whiskey with sweet vermouth and orange bitters make up this historic cocktail recipe.
instructions:
1. Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
2. Stir until chilled.
3. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
4. Garnish with a lemon or orange twist.

name: Chocolate Martica
description: This simple variation on a modern classic from 2007 was one of the first to tap chocolate bitters’ flavor potential.
instructions: Stir all of the ingredients with ice, then strain into a chilled glass.

name: Chrysanthemum
description: Hard to spell but easy to drink, the Chrysanthemum falls into the category of lesser-known classics—still held in good regard, but not often invited to the party. However, with a formula that ticks the current trendy cocktail boxes, the Chrysanthemum might just be ready to bloom once more. Debuting more than a century ago, the recipe first appeared in 1916, followed by an adaptation in 1930. Eschewing a base spirit altogether, the Chrysanthemum puts vermouth in the spotlight, augmented with herbal liqueur Bénédictine and boosted by a few dashes of absinthe. When absinthe was legalized in the U.S. at the end of 2006, a lot of bartenders went looking for golden age recipes, prompting the drink’s initial resurgence within the craft cocktail renaissance. The primary variation is seen in the ratio of the cocktail, evolving over thedecades in step with drinkers’ tastes. While the early recipe called for equal parts dry vermouth and Bénédictine, the 1930 version dialed back the sweetness with a 2:1 ratio, which remains more or less the standard today.
instructions:
1. Stir all of the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice until chilled. Strain into a chilled glass and garnish.
2. Tip: Try this with blanc vermouth, as many of the recipes of this era like the Algonquin, El Presidente, and Blackthorn that call for dry vermouth taste better with blanc vermouth.

name: Ciderhouse Mule
description: Taking the Moscow Mule into spritz territory, this drink combines vodka, lime, and ginger syrup with a touch of raspberry liqueur and sparkling rosé.
instructions:
1. Add all of the ingredients, except the sparkling rosé, to a shaker with ice.
2. Shake until chilled.
3. Add the sparkling rosé to the shaker before straining the cocktail into a glass filled with ice.
4. Garnish.

name: Cinder Bloom
description: Using the Margarita as a template, this cocktail layers the bold flavors of passion fruit and Aperol with the sweet vegetal notes of ají peppers for a refreshing and aromatic cocktail. Any tropical pepper will work, too, or swap in red or yellow bell peppers for a more vegetal profile.
instructions: 1. Place 4 ají dulce peppers in a shaker and muddle. Add the rest of the ingredients along with ice. Shake hard for about 5 seconds, or until the outside of the shaker is frosty. Strain into the glass over ice.

name: Clarified New York Sour
description: This clarified take on the New York Sour achieves a silky mouthfeel and a softened acidity, making for an easy-drinking sipper.
instructions:
1. Combine the bourbon, lemon, and simple syrup and pour over the milk in a glass container.
2. Let sit for 30 minutes, allowing the milk to curdle.
3. Strain the milk mixture through a coffee filter.
4. If it’s not clear, re-pour through the same filter.
5. To serve, pour the mixture over a large ice cube in a glass.
6. Float with red wine.

name: Clover Club
description: The Clover Club Cocktail is a drink that pre-dates Prohibition in the United States, and is named for the Philadelphia men's club of the same name, which met in the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel at South Broad and Walnut Streets in Center City. The Clover Club was chartered in 1882.
instructions:
1. Pour all ingredients into cocktails shaker.
2. Shake well with ice.
3. Strain into chilled cocktail glass.

The egg white is not added for the purpose of giving the drink flavor, but rather acts as an emulsifier. Thus when the drink is shaken a characteristic foamy head is formed.

name: Clover Leaf
description: This recipe is a modern take on a century-old relative of the Clover Club cocktail, utilizing a base of gin and Chambord to create a berry-forward delight.
instructions:
1. Combine the Chambord or grenadine, lemon juice, egg white or half-and-half, and gin in a cocktail shaker with ice cubes.
2. Shake vigorously for 10 seconds, until the ingredients are cold and the mix is frothy with a pink blush.
3. Strain into a Martini or coupe cocktail glass, making sure there is a thin layer of foam and a few small ice chips floating on top.
4. Garnish with the mint leaf.

name: Coconut Nuclear Daiquiri
description: The nuclear Daiquiri cocktail recipe combines rum, green Chartreuse, coconut syrup and lime juice.
instructions:
1. Add all ingredients in a shaker and hard shake with ice.
2. Double-strain into Nick and Nora glass.

name: Coffee & Cigarettes
description: This riff on a Manhattan / Rob Roy features an Islay Whisky which provides a rich smokiness that compliments the coffee & cacao notes.I highly recommend trying this one!
instructions:
1. Combine the ingredients into your mixing glass
2. Stir with ice for 30-40 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled stemmed cocktail glass

name: Coffee Cocktail
description:
It probably would be difficult to come up with a more misleading name for this cocktail, than Coffee Cocktail. It does not feature coffee or have anything in common with it, unless you consider coffee to be delicious (which I do by the way) and this cocktail is certainly also delicious to the very last drop.

Base of this cocktail is Tawny Port, the aged nature of wine bringing notes of nuts, dried fruits and hint of rich sweetness. It is then paired with oak and vanilla tones of the cognac, increasing the overall cocktail complexity, while at the same time increasing proof. As a true flip requires, a whole egg is added, turning this cocktail into what it is, a rich and decadent indulgence. The creamy texture makes this cocktail especially suited for the holiday season. In the end, a touch of simple syrup helps with the balance and enables delicious individual notes pop to the forefront, while freshly grated nutmeg garnish adds a further aromatic dimension.

All in all, Coffee Cocktail might not have anything in common with its namesake, but it is a tasty and decadent drink, seemingly made for the holiday season.
instructions:
1. Combine all of the ingredients in a cocktail shaker.
2. Dry shake to emulsify the egg.
3. Add ice and shake until chilled.
4. Double strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
garnish: Garnish with some freshly grated nutmeg.

name: Coffee Enzoni
description: The Enzoni is a personal favorite of mine. I first shared it in 2020 and the video has received almost 700,000 views (other people love it too!). I also featured it more recently in my top 3 cocktails video a few weeks ago before stumbling across a caffeinated version. I knew I had to try it immediately and it did not disappoint!The Coffee Enzoni is a pretty straight forward variation on the original Enzoni with the use of black grapes (sable grapes if available) instead of green, and the addition of coffee liqueur. Whilst the original Enzoni is bright and bitter, the Coffee Enzoni is dark, rich and brooding. It features rich bitter coffee notes and a juicy, muscat grape flavor.Worth noting... the original version used an extra dry coffee liqueur with 100g of sugar per litre. Mr Black has 250g per litre. For comparison, Kahlua has 400g per litre. As a result, it adds 10 ml of a 2:1 light muscovado syrup to balance the drink. Because I used Mr Black, the additional syrup isn't required.
instructions:
1. In a cocktail shaker, muddle the grapes
2. Add the remaining ingredients
3. Shake with ice for 10-12 seconds
4. Double strain over ice into an old fashioned glass
5. Garnish with 3 skewered black grapes

name: Coffee Julep
description: Coffee liqueur and Demerara Gum Syrup give this Julep a jolt of rich flavor.
instructions:
1. Muddle 5-10 mint leaves with syrup in a julep cup
2. Fill with crushed ice and add bourbon and coffee liqueur
3. Stir until cold and frosty, then top with more crushed ice
4. Smack a mint sprig between your hands to express its oils, then garnish

name: Coffee Negroni
description: It’s commonly been said that the only thing better than a Negroni is a Coffee Negroni. And considering the drink is an equal part mix of Coffee Liqueur, Campari & Gin, we’ve got to agree.
instructions: Stir all ingredients in an ice-filled mixing glass, then strain into an ice-filled rocks glass

name: Cold Brew Americano
description: This Americano cocktail recipe combines the Italian cocktail and the espresso drink for a bitter, low-proof serve.
instructions:
1. Fill a Collins glass with ice. Add the first four ingredients and stir.
2. Top with seltzer, then garnish with half an orange wheel.

name: Cold Brew White Russian
description: Fans of the White Russian will love this richer, creamier take on the classic coffee cocktail. This version backs up the traditional coffee liqueur with cold-brew coffee and vanilla syrup for balanced depth. And instead of a straight dose of heavy cream, it's shaken with simple syrup to up the decadence even more.
instructions:
1. Put a glass in the freezer for at least 30 minutes before preparing the cocktail. Combine the vodka, coffee liqueur, coffee, and vanilla syrup with ice and shake to chill, then set aside.
2. Fill the chilled glass with large ice cubes. Add the foam cream to the bottom of the glass over ice, filling a 1/3 of the glass. Carefully pour the prepared cocktail base over the foam cream for a rich, layered presentation.
3. Foam CreamCombine 8 parts of heavy cream with 1 part of simple syrup (1:1)  in a shaker. Shake until thickened but still pourable.

name: Comte de Sureau
description: The name translates to count of elderflower, which is a nod to the St-Germain that acts as the floral sweetener here.
instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled rocks glass over ice.
garnish: Garnish with orange and lemon twists.

name: Conference Cocktail
description: Tiki was jealous of the Old Fashioned build, and the Conference cocktail was born.
instructions:
1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice
2. Stir 20 seconds and strain into a chilled rocks glass with ice.

name: Coronado Cocktail
description: The combination of Tropical Passionfruit Syrup, coconut water, and tequila has tropical written all over it.
instructions:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker
2. Add ice and shake hard for 10 seconds
3. Strain into a highball glass over crushed ice
4. Garnish with a lemon wheel

name: Corpse Reviver №2
description: The Corpse Reviver №2 is the most commonly drunk of the corpse revivers, and consists of equal parts gin, lemon juice, curaçao (commonly Cointreau), Kina Lillet (now usually replaced with Cocchi Americano, as a closer match to Kina Lillet than modern Lillet Blanc), and a dash of absinthe. The dash of absinthe can either be added to the mix before shaking, or added to the cocktail glass and moved around until the glass has been coated with a layer of absinthe to give a subtle absinthe aroma and flavor to the drink.
instructions: Pour all ingredients into shaker with ice. Shake well and strain in chilled cocktail glass.

name: Cosa Nostra №2
description: A delicious and simple Highball
instructions:
Shake everything except the ginger ale with ice and strain into a pilsner glass over crushed ice.
Top with the ginger ale

name: Cosmopolitan
description:
A cosmopolitan, or informally a cosmo, is a relative of cranberry coolers.

The cosmopolitan gained popularity in the 1990s. It was further popularized among young women by its frequent mention on the television program Sex and the City, where Sarah Jessica Parker's character, Carrie Bradshaw, commonly ordered the drink when out with her girlfriends. The film adaptation made a reference to its popularity when Miranda asks why they stopped drinking them, Carrie replies "because everyone else started."
instructions: Add all ingredients into a cocktail shaker filled with ice. Shake well and strain into a large cocktail glass.

name: Countermand
description: The Countermand is a mini reverse Martini cocktail recipe. It's made with gin, maraschino and absinthe.
instructions:
1. Combine all ingredients in a chilled, petite glass with one large ice cube.
2. Stir briefly, then express a lemon coin over the drink and discard.

name: Creole Gimlet
description: Falernum adds hints of Caribbean Island flavors for a tasty twist on the classic Gimlet. The touch of Caribbean spice makes you want to dance to island music.
instructions:
1. Add all ingredients to a shaker and shake.
2. Double strain into a chilled Coupe glass.
3. Garnish with lime wheel.

name: Cuba Libre
description:
The cocktail originated in the early 20th century in Cuba, after the country won independence in the Spanish–American War. It subsequently became popular across Cuba, the United States, and other countries. Its simple recipe and inexpensive, ubiquitous ingredients have made it one of the world's most-popular alcoholic drinks. Drink critics often consider the drink mediocre, but it has been noted for its historical significance.

Traditionally, the cola ingredient is Coca-Cola ("Coke") and the alcohol is a light rum such as Bacardi; however, the drink may be made with various types of rums and cola brands, and lime juice may or may not be included.
instructions: Build all ingredients in a highball glass filled with ice.

name: Cucumber Gimlet
instructions: Combine all ingredients and shake with ice. Serve in a rocks glass over crushed ice. Garnish with a rolled cucumber slice.

name: Cynar Flip
description: A magnificent application of Cynar in the holiday canon
instructions:
1. Dry shake the whole egg in a cocktail shaker
2. Add Cynar, simple syrup, and ice before shaking again
3. Strain into a cocktail glass and drop several dashes of the bitters into the foam

name: Daiquiri
description: Daiquirí is also the name of a beach and an iron mine near Santiago de Cuba, and is a word of Taíno origin. The drink was supposedly invented by an American mining engineer who was in Cuba (then at the tail-end of the Spanish Captaincy-General government) at the time of the Spanish–American War. It is also possible that a US congressman who purchased the Santiago iron mines in 1902 introduced the daiquiri to clubs in New York in that year.
instructions:
1. In a cocktail shaker add all ingredients.
2. Stir well to dissolve the sugar.
3. Add ice and shake.
4. Strain into chilled cocktail glass.

name: Daiquiri #4
description: A frozen Daiquiri cocktail recipe, also known as the Hemingway Daiquiri, after the author who was known to drink them.
instructions:
1. Blend all ingredients with a scoop of crushed ice for 15 seconds.
2. Pour into an 8 1/2-ounce coupe glass.
3. Serve with straws.

name: Dark ‘n’ stormy
description:
This drink is very similar to the Moscow mule except that the Dark 'n' Stormy has dark rum instead of vodka. The original Dark 'n' Stormy was made with Gosling Black Seal rum and Barritt's Ginger Beer, but after the partnership between the two failed and the companies parted ways, Gosling Brothers created its own ginger beer.

Gosling Brothers claims that the drink was invented in Bermuda just after World War I.
instructions: In a highball glass filled with ice pour the ginger beer and top floating with the Rum.
garnish: Garnish with a lime wedge or slice.

name: Day-O’ Fashioned
description: The Day-O’ Fashioned is a tropical Old-Fashioned cocktail recipe made with rye whiskey, rum, banana liqueur, cold brew, orange and Angostura.
instructions:
1. In a rocks glass, muddle the orange peel with the bitters.
2. Add the rest of the ingredients and ice, and stir gently until well-chilled.
3. Garnish with an orange slice and a black cherry.

name: Dead Man's Handle
description: This summery tequila cocktail gets punched up with Aperol and perfectly sweetened with orgeat.
instructions: Combine, Shake with Ice. Top with a sprinkle of Tajín seasoning.

name: Dead Sea Mule
description: A house-made pomegranate grenadine is the key to the Dead Sea Mule, a mezcal-laced twist on the classic Moscow Mule.
instructions:
1. Fill a Collins glass with ice, then add the mezcal, lime juice and grenadine.
2. Top with the ginger beer and stir briefly and gently to combine.
3. Garnish with the mint sprig and 2 skewered pieces of candied ginger.

name: Death Flip
description:
When this cocktail first appeared on a menu in Melbourne, in 2010, no ingredients were listed. And if you asked what was in the drink, the bartender would not tell you. The only thing offering the customer a hint as to what they were getting into was the ominous description: “You don’t wanna meet this cocktail in a dark alley.”

Of course, plenty of people stepped up to take the bait, and many ended up liking the cocktail—something that likely wouldn’t have happened if the ingredients were listed: tequila, yellow Chartreuse, Jägermeister and a whole egg. To date, it is the only flip to become a modern classic.
instructions: 1. Combine all ingredients in a mixing tin and shake with ice. Strain into a sour glass.

name: Debbie, Don't
description: An adventurous modern cocktail for those with a limited bar
instructions:
1. Combine all ingredients over ice and shake
2. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass, serve up

name: Deep South
description: Our peach syrup, with a split base of mezcal and rye whiskey, adds a summer note to this whiskey sour.
instructions:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker
2. Add ice and shake hard for 20 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled rocks glass

name: Delta T
description: A cocktail designed to highlight the unique buttery and funky notes of Variable Dunderclap rum, balanced by the sharpness of ginger and the herbaceous qualities of Fernet. It's a complex, easy-sipping drink that plays with contrasts of hot and cold flavors.
instructions:
1. Add all ingredients except ginger beer to a shaking tin.
2. Add ice and shake until chilled.
3. Strain into a highball glass over an ice spear.
4. Top with ginger beer.
5. Add several dashes of Angostura bitters on top.
garnish: candied ginger, lime peel, and a fresh bunch of mint

name: Diki-Diki
description: A revived golden-era cocktail and fabulous way to tinker with Swedish Punsch
instructions:
1. Combine all ingredients over ice and shake
2. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass, serve up

name: Dirty Martini
description: The Dirty Martini is a popular cocktail that adds olive brine to the classic Martini, giving it a savory flavor. It can be made with either gin or vodka, depending on personal preference.
instructions:
1. Select and pre-chill a Martini glass.
2. Prepare garnish of skewered Green Olives.
3. Stir all ingredients with ice.
4. Strain into chilled glass.
5. Garnish with skewered olives.

name: Disgruntled Mai Tai
description: The Disgruntled Mai Tai is a spin on the rum tiki drink that adds Aperol and a bottle of bitter Underberg to the cocktail.
instructions:
1. Combine all ingredients except for the Underberg in a cocktail shaker.
2. Briefly dry shake without ice, then add a few small ice cubes and shake until the ice has melted.
3. Pour into a chilled rocks glass and top with crushed ice.
4. Remove the cap and the top of the paper wrapper on the Underberg bottle and insert it, upside-down, into the crushed ice.
5. Garnish with a mint sprig, lime wedge, grated nutmeg and a cocktail umbrella.
garnish: mint sprig, lime wedge, freshly grated nutmeg, cocktail umbrella

name: Division Bell
description: Mezcal takes the place of gin and Aperol that of Chartreuse in this simple riff on the Last Word.
instructions:
1. Combine all ingredients in a cocktail shaker with ice and shake until chilled.
2. Strain into a coupe.
3. Express a grapefruit twist over the surface of the drink, then discard.

name: Don Lockwood
description: A chocolate, smoky riff on the old fashioned that proves simple variations on classic cocktails can have impressive results. This is one of my favourite modern classic cocktails.
instructions:
1. In a mixing glass combine all ingredients
2. Stir with ice for 20-30 seconds
3. Strain over ice into an old fashioned glass

name: Doubleplusgood
description:
Doubleplusgood is a take on a Mai Tai, crossed with a Pisco Sour. It’s mildly sweet, with the gentle almond flavor of orgeat laced through the delicate foam of egg white (or aquafaba, if you prefer).

The garnish is a signature of the recipe: two plus signs, drawn in the foam with aromatic bitters.
instructions: Dry-shake all ingredients (except the bitters) first without ice, then again with ice added. Double-strain through a fine mesh strainer into a chilled short glass, no ice. Drop the bitters atop the foam in the shape of two plus symbols.
garnish: two plus signs, drawn in the foam with aromatic bitters

name: Dreamy Dorini Smoking Martini
description: This Vodka Martini riff is anything but ordinary, with peaty single malt scotch and Pernod taking the place of dry vermouth and orange bitters.
instructions:
1. Add all ingredients into a mixing glass with ice and stir until well-chilled.
2. Strain into a cocktail glass.
3. Express the oils from the lemon twist over the drink, then garnish with the twist.

name: Drifter
description: This cocktail, the Drifter, is a straightforward mixture of Japanese whisky, blanc vermouth, Amaro Nonino and Peychaud’s bitters, garnished with a grapefruit twist.
instructions:
1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice and stir gently.
2. Strain into a double rocks glass over a large ice cube.
3. Garnish with a grapefruit twist.

name: Drunk Uncle
description:
Drunk Uncle is a cocktail inspired by a negroni, specifically a scotch negroni, with bold, strong bitter-sweet and boozy taste profile. Although in my mind it has left the true negroni specs in order to explore a more inventive and just as delicious direction.

As you probably guessed base spirit of this cocktail is a scotch, in this particular case smoky and funky Islay scotch takes the centre stage. It is then paired with Cynar, a bitter-sweet artichoke liqueur with deep flavours balanced by the subtle vegetal and herbal notes. For me it plays incredibly well with Islay scotch, probably even better than Campari would. Addition of bianco vermouth brings a touch more sweetness and delicate herbaceousness to the mix binding the cocktail into a delicious whole. Last, but not least, grapefruit peel serves not only as an eye-catching garnish, but also expands the aromatic dimension of the cocktail, giving it a light, fresh citrusy touch.

All in all, Drunk Uncle is my kind of negroni, dark, bold and full of amazing flavour. I might be partial here, since I love Cynar, but for me there is no better negroni variation for these cold and dark winter evenings.
instructions:
1. Combine all of the ingredients in a mixing glass.
2. Add ice and stir for 30-45 sec. or approx. 60 revolutions.
3. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
garnish: Garnish with a twist of grapefruit.

name: E Tonico
description: E Tonico is a Gin & Tonic with an Italian twist courtesy of an aperitivo liqueur, vermouth and saline solution.
instructions:
1. Combine the first five ingredients in a Collins glass and fill with ice.
2. Top with tonic water.
3. Garnish with a bay leaf.
